Before the formulas

How to read the maths in this course (plain words)

read once, refer back

Every formula in DIP is built from about twenty symbols. Here is each one in words, with a tiny example you can check in your head. When a formula looks scary, read it aloud using this table.

SymbolSay it asTiny example
\(f(x,y)\)the brightness of the pixel in row x, column y (rows go down, columns go right, both start at 0)f(0,0) = top-left pixel; f(2,1) = third row, second column
\(M_f(i,j)\)the same image written as a matrix, but counted from 1 (your instructor’s convention)\(M_f(2,2)=f(1,1)\)
\(r_k,\ n_k,\ p_r(r_k)\)subscript k = “number k in the list”: the k-th grey level, how many pixels have it, and that count ÷ total pixelsn₃ = 360 → 360 pixels have level 3
\(L,\ L-1\)L = how many grey levels there are; L − 1 = the brightest level3-bit: L = 8, levels 0…7
\(\sum_{j=0}^{k}a_j\)“add up aj for j = 0, 1, …, k” — a running total\(\sum_{j=0}^{2}j=0+1+2=3\)
\(\sum_{s=-1}^{1}\sum_{t=-1}^{1}\)two running totals inside each other = add over all 9 positions of a 3×3 windowthe centre is s = t = 0
\(|x|\)size of x, ignoring its sign|−3| = 3; for a complex number |a + bi| = √(a² + b²)
\(\max(a,b),\ \min(a,b)\)the larger / smaller of the twomax(3, 6) = 6
\(\lfloor x\rfloor\), round(x)floor = drop the decimals (go down); round = nearest whole number (.5 goes up)⌊3.7⌋ = 3, round(3.5) = 4
\(\in,\ \notin\)“is one of”, “is not one of”\(r\in\{0,\dots,7\}\)
\(A\cup B,\ A\cap B,\ A^c\)union (either/max), intersection (both/min), complement (everything not in A / L−1−z)grey images: union = pixelwise max
\(\mapsto\), \(\to\)“is sent to” — what a transformation does to one value\(r\mapsto L-1-r\) is the negative
\(T(r),\ s=T(r)\)a rule that turns an input grey level r into an output level sT(r) = 7 − r
\(w\star f,\ w*f\)correlation (slide w as printed), convolution (rotate w by 180° first)they are equal for symmetric kernels
\(f\circledast h\)circular convolution: indices wrap around (mod n)index −1 means n − 1
\(A\odot B\)multiply matching entries (not the matrix product)\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\end{bmatrix}\odot\begin{bmatrix}3&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&8\end{bmatrix}\)
\(A^T\), \(A^{-1}\)transpose (rows become columns); inverse (the matrix that undoes A)\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\end{bmatrix}^T\) is a column
\(\nabla^2 f\)“del squared f”, the Laplacian: how much a pixel differs from its neighbours (sum of neighbours − 4 × pixel)flat area → 0
\(\nabla f\), \(\partial f/\partial x\)gradient: the slope of brightness; ∂/∂x = slope going down the rowsf(x+1, y) − f(x, y)
\(\sigma,\ \sigma^2,\ m,\ \bar z\)standard deviation (spread), variance (spread²), mean (average)mean of 2, 4 = 3; σ = 1
\(e^{-j2\pi ux/M}\), \(W_n\)a unit arrow turned by −360°·ux/M (Euler: cos θ − j sin θ); Wn = e−j2π/n\(W_4=-j\)
\(F(u,v)\), \(|F|\), \(\phi\)the DFT value at frequency (u, v), its size, its angleF(0,0) = sum of all pixels (slides’ DFT)
\(\propto,\ \approx\)grows in proportion to; is roughly
\(\forall,\ \Rightarrow,\ \iff\)for every; therefore/implies; if and only if
Reading strategy. (1) Find what is being computed (left of “=”). (2) Find what changes in the sum (the letter under Σ). (3) Write the first two terms out in full with numbers. After two terms the pattern is obvious and the symbols stop being scary.

Chapters 1–2.3 · Lectures 1–4

What an image is, how we see it, and how a camera makes it

TB 1, 2.1–2.3slides: Overview; Fundamentals pp. 3–19theory + one-line numbers

The easiest marks in the paper: short facts and one-line calculations. This section explains what a digital image is, which kinds of radiation make images, how the human eye forms and perceives an image (and where it is fooled), and how a camera sensor captures one. The numbers you may be asked for: the size of an image on the retina, a wavelength from a frequency, and resolution of a camera.

1What is a (digital) image, and what is DIP?

An image is a function: give it a position (x, y) and it returns a brightness f(x, y). For a colour image it returns three numbers (red, green, blue). Digital means both the positions and the brightness values are whole-number steps; each little square is a pixel.

Digital image processing = using a computer to process, analyse and interpret images. Your slides split it into three levels:

LevelInput → outputExamples
Lowimage → imageremove noise, sharpen, increase contrast
Midimage → attributesfind edges, segment objects, extract features
High (computer vision)image → meaning / decisionrecognise a face, classify an object

This course covers the low and mid levels.

Why computers could do it (slide history): the von Neumann architecture (1945: memory, arithmetic-logic unit, control unit, input, output), the transistor (Bell Labs, 1948), high-level languages and the integrated circuit (1950s–60s), Intel’s microprocessor (1970s), the IBM PC (1981), and ever smaller chips (LSI → VLSI → ULSI).

2Where images come from: the electromagnetic spectrum

Most images are made by some kind of electromagnetic (EM) radiation. The bands differ only in wavelength — and each band shows different things, which is why each has its own uses.

  • Gamma rays: nuclear medicine (a radioactive tracer shows tumours and bone infections), astronomy, cargo screening.
  • X-rays: CT (computerised tomography) scans, baggage screening.
  • Ultraviolet: fluorescence microscopy (cells, proteins), astronomy.
  • Visible and infrared: everyday cameras, biometrics, licence plates, inspection, satellites; IR for night vision, missile tracking.
  • Microwaves: radar (it sees through clouds and darkness), ground-penetrating radar, industrial inspection.
  • Radio: MRI, radio astronomy, long-range radar.
  • Not EM at all: ultrasound (sound waves — pregnancy scans, heart, abdomen, muscles) and electron microscopy (a beam of electrons).

Memory hook: “Gamma, X, UV, Visible, IR, Microwave, Radio” — energy falls from left to right.

Where you use it: one-line theory questions (“give an application of X-ray / microwave imaging”).

3The eye, part by part

Light goes cornea → pupil → lens → retina; the retina turns it into nerve signals that travel along the optic nerve to the brain. Each part has a camera equivalent.

PartWhat it doesCamera equivalent
Corneaclear dome at the front; protects and bends (focuses) lightfront glass
Iris and pupilthe coloured ring and the hole in it; the hole’s size controls how much light entersaperture
Lens + ciliary musclesthe muscles change the lens’s shape to focus near or farfocusing lens
Retinalight-sensitive layer with rods and conessensor
Fovea (macula)≈ 1.5 mm centre of the retina, packed with cones: sharp, colour visionthe sharpest part of the sensor
Blind spot (optic disc)where the optic nerve leaves: no rods or cones, no image—
Sclerathe white tough outer coatcamera body
Light path: cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → brain. Ciliary muscles reshape the lens to focus; the sclera is the white protective coat.

Rods and cones

RodsCones
How many≈ 90–120 million≈ 6–7 million
Whereall over, none in the foveapacked in the fovea
Light neededvery little (they work in the dark)bright light
Visionscotopic (night), no colourphotopic (day), colour
Detaillow: many rods share one nerve endhigh: one cone per nerve end

Three cone types: L (long wavelength, red-ish, 60–65 %), M (medium, green, 30–35 %), S (short, blue, 5–10 %). L and M are coded on the X chromosome, S on chromosome 7 — with two X chromosomes, women more often have an extra L/M variant, the slide’s explanation for better colour discrimination.

Where you use it: “Compare rods and cones”, “what is the fovea / blind spot”. Memory hook: rods = night, many, blurry; cones = colour, few, sharp.

4How big is the image on the retina? (similar triangles)

The lens makes a small upside-down image on the retina. The object, the lens and its image form two similar triangles, so the ratios are equal.

\(\dfrac{\text{object height}}{\text{object distance}}=\dfrac{\text{image height}}{\text{lens-to-retina distance}}\)In the eye the lens-to-retina distance is fixed at about 17 mm; the eye focuses by changing the lens shape (focal length). A camera does the opposite: fixed focal length, the sensor distance changes.

Example (your slide). A 15 m palm tree 100 m away: 15/100 = h/17 → h = 17 × 0.15 = 2.55 mm (the slide writes 2.5 mm).

The same triangle answers the camera questions (textbook 2.6, 2.8) with the camera’s focal length in place of 17 mm, and the smallest-visible-dot question (2.2).

Where you use it: slide example, textbook 2.2, 2.6, 2.8. Keep both distances in the same units.

Textbook 2.2 (homework)

Smallest printed dot the eye can see at 0.2 m

Model the fovea as a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm square holding 337,000 cones, with cones and the spaces between them equally wide. The eye stops seeing a dot when its image on the fovea is smaller than one cone. Thinking purely geometrically (lens–retina distance 17 mm), what is the diameter of the smallest dot you can see on a page 0.2 m away?
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here
  1. √(337000) → 580.517; then 2×Ans−1EXE → 1160.03.
  2. 1.5÷Ans×200÷17EXE → 0.0152 (mm).
Final answer
Cone (and gap) width ≈ 1.5 mm ÷ 1160 ≈ 1.29 µm, so the smallest dot ≈ 0.2 m × 1.29 µm ÷ 17 mm ≈ 0.0152 mm (about 15 µm).
Full solution
Concept
Two separate pictures: (1) how big is one cone? (count how many cones fit along one side of the square), (2) what object size makes an image that big? (the palm-tree triangle again).
Formula
\(\dfrac{\text{object size}}{\text{object distance}}=\dfrac{\text{image size}}{17\ \text{mm}}\)
1
Cones per side of the square: \(\sqrt{337000}=580.5\).
2
Cones and gaps are equally wide, so along one side there are 580.5 cones and 579.5 gaps ≈ \(2(580.5)-1\approx1160\) equal pieces. One piece \(=1.5/1160 = 1.293\times10^{-3}\) mm \(=1.29\ \mu\)m. That is the cone diameter.
3
The dot is seen only if its image is at least one cone wide: \(\dfrac{x}{0.2\ \text{m}}=\dfrac{1.293\ \mu\text{m}}{17\ \text{mm}}\Rightarrow x = 200\ \text{mm}\times\dfrac{1.293\times10^{-3}\ \text{mm}}{17\ \text{mm}}=0.0152\) mm.
Answer
Cone (and gap) width ≈ 1.5 mm ÷ 1160 ≈ 1.29 µm, so the smallest dot ≈ 0.2 m × 1.29 µm ÷ 17 mm ≈ 0.0152 mm (about 15 µm).
Faster in the exam
  • Keep everything in mm: 0.2 m = 200 mm.
  • Aim for 4:15 (allotment 5:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Using 580 cones per side without the gaps (that doubles the cone size).
  • Forgetting that the eye’s image distance is fixed at 17 mm.

5Brightness is not what the eye reports

The eye does not measure light like a meter. It adapts to the average light level, and the brightness we perceive depends on the surroundings. Four effects from your slides:

Brightness adaptation

The eye handles an enormous range of light (about 1010 to 1), but not all at once: it shifts its sensitivity to the current level and only then distinguishes a small range around it. Perceived brightness grows roughly like the log of the light intensity.

Weber ratio ΔIc/I

On a background of intensity I, ΔIc is the smallest extra brightness you notice half the time. Small ratio = good discrimination. Example: I = 100, ΔIc = 2 → 0.02 (good). In dim light (rods) the ratio is large; in bright light (cones) small.

Mach bands

Next to each edge we see a dark and a light stripe that are not there — the visual system exaggerates edges.

Simultaneous contrast

The same grey looks darker on a white background and lighter on a black one: perceived brightness depends on the surroundings.

Optical illusions (your slide) are the same idea: the brain fills in or distorts what the eye receives.

Where you use it: theory questions (“explain Mach bands / simultaneous contrast / what a low Weber ratio means”).

6Light: wavelength, frequency, energy

All EM radiation travels at the speed of light c. A wave that wiggles faster (higher frequency) has a shorter wavelength and carries more energy per photon.

\(c=\lambda\,\nu\)speed = wavelength × frequency, c = 2.998 × 108 m/s. So λ = c/ν.
\(E=h\,\nu\)energy of one photon = Planck’s constant × frequency.

Example (textbook 2.3). 60 Hz mains electricity: λ = 2.998 × 108 / 60 = 5.0 × 106 m ≈ 5000 km.

Visible light is about 0.43 µm (violet) to 0.79 µm (red). Radio waves are about 109 times longer than visible light; gamma rays about 107 times shorter.

Light words: radiance = energy leaving the source; luminance = how much of it an observer perceives; brightness = the subjective impression. Light with no colour is monochromatic; its only property is intensity, measured in grey levels from black to white.

Colour models: RGB adds coloured light to black (screens); CMYK starts from white paper and adds inks that absorb light (printing); HSV/HSI describes colour as hue (which colour), saturation (how strong) and value/intensity (how bright) — handy for processing.

7How a camera captures an image

An image needs a source of energy, a scene that reflects or lets it through, and a sensor that turns the arriving energy into a voltage. Then sampling and quantisation (Section 2.4) turn the voltage into numbers.

Three sensor arrangements:

  • Single sensor (a photodiode): one value at a time, so the sensor (or the scene) must move in both x and y. Slow but precise (high-precision scanners).
  • Strip of sensors: one whole line at a time; moving perpendicular to the strip gives the second direction (flatbed scanners, airborne imaging). A ring of sensors around the body plus reconstruction gives CT slices.
  • 2-D array (CCD or CMOS): the whole image at once — every digital camera. Each element’s response is proportional to the total light it collected. CMOS sensors read out faster and use less power than CCDs.

Colour: each sensor element sits under one colour filter (the Bayer pattern), so it measures only red, only green or only blue. Demosaicing fills in the two missing colours at every pixel from its neighbours.

Twice as many green filters because the eye is most sensitive to green. Larger sensors (full frame 864 mm², crop factor 1) gather more light than a phone sensor (≈ 70 mm², crop factor ≈ 3.5).

Illumination × reflectance

\(f(x,y)=i(x,y)\cdot r(x,y)\), with \(0what the camera records = light falling on the point × the fraction the point reflects.

Example. A white wall (r = 0.80) on a sunny day (i = 90,000 lx) gives f = 72,000; the same wall under a full moon (i = 0.1 lx) gives f = 0.08. Black velvet (r = 0.01) in the sun gives 900. This huge range is why cameras (and eyes) must adapt.

Where you use it: theory (“how is a 2-D image acquired with a single sensor / strip / array?”, “what is demosaicing?”), and textbook 2.4, 2.6, 2.8 below.
Textbook 2.4 (homework)

Which light and camera to image cells, bacteria, viruses and proteins?

Specimens have sizes 50 mm (cells), 1 mm (bacteria), 0.1 mm (viruses) and 0.01 mm (proteins). The smallest detail to be seen on any specimen is 0.001 mm. Light can only “see” things at least as large as its wavelength. (a) Can one illumination source and one camera do it? If yes, which band? (b) If not, what would you use?
Final answer
Needed detail = 0.001 mm = 1 µm, so the illumination wavelength must be ≤ 1 µm. Visible light (0.43–0.79 µm) satisfies this for every specimen, so (a) yes: visible-band illumination with a camera sensitive in the visible band (with suitable magnification/optics, e.g. a microscope for the small specimens). (b) does not arise. (Ultraviolet, shorter than visible, would also work but is not needed.)
Full solution
Concept
“To see a detail, the wavelength must be the same size or smaller than the detail.” So the deciding number is the smallest detail (1 µm), not the specimen sizes.
1
Smallest detail: 0.001 mm = 1 µm.
2
Bands with λ ≤ 1 µm: visible (≈ 0.43–0.79 µm), UV, X-ray, gamma. The cheapest and most common choice is visible light.
3
One visible source and one visible-band camera therefore resolve 1 µm on every specimen; only the optics (magnification) change between a 50 mm cell and a 0.01 mm protein.
Answer
Needed detail = 0.001 mm = 1 µm, so the illumination wavelength must be ≤ 1 µm. Visible light (0.43–0.79 µm) satisfies this for every specimen, so (a) yes: visible-band illumination with a camera sensitive in the visible band (with suitable magnification/optics, e.g. a microscope for the small specimens). (b) does not arise. (Ultraviolet, shorter than visible, would also work but is not needed.)
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 3:15 (allotment 4:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Choosing the band from the specimen size (e.g. 50 mm → radio) instead of from the 1 µm detail.
Textbook 2.6

Line pairs per mm a CCD camera can resolve

A 7 mm × 7 mm CCD chip with 1024 × 1024 elements, a 35 mm lens, viewing a flat square area 0.5 m away. How many line pairs per mm can it resolve? (Model the camera like the eye: lens focal length in place of the 17 mm.)
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here
7×500÷35EXE → 100; 1024÷Ans÷2EXE → 5.12
Final answer
The chip sees a 100 mm × 100 mm area; 1024 elements over 100 mm = 10.24 elements/mm; one line pair needs 2 elements → ≈ 5.12 lp/mm (≈ 5 lp/mm).
Full solution
Concept
Similar triangles map the chip (7 mm) back onto the scene: chip size / focal length = scene size / distance. Then count elements per mm on the scene. A line pair = one dark + one light line = 2 pixels.
1
Scene width \(x\): \(\dfrac{x}{500}=\dfrac{7}{35}\Rightarrow x=100\) mm.
2
1024 elements across 100 mm → 10.24 elements per mm.
3
Line pairs per mm = 10.24 ÷ 2 = 5.12.
Answer
The chip sees a 100 mm × 100 mm area; 1024 elements over 100 mm = 10.24 elements/mm; one line pair needs 2 elements → ≈ 5.12 lp/mm (≈ 5 lp/mm).
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 3:15 (allotment 4:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the ÷2 (a line pair is two pixels).
Textbook 2.8

Choose a CCD chip for 5 line pairs per mm

An application needs 5 line pairs per mm on a 0.5 m × 0.5 m area that is 1 m from a 200 mm lens. What is the minimum number of sensing elements and the chip size d × d?
Final answer
5 lp/mm = 10 pixels/mm on the object → 500 mm × 10 = 5000 × 5000 elements; chip side d = 500 mm × 200/1000 = 100 mm (a 100 mm × 100 mm chip).
Full solution
1
Each line pair needs 2 pixels: 5 lp/mm → 10 pixels per mm of the object.
2
0.5 m = 500 mm per side → 500 × 10 = 5000 elements per side.
3
Chip size by similar triangles: \(d/200 = 500/1000\Rightarrow d=100\) mm.
Answer
5 lp/mm = 10 pixels/mm on the object → 500 mm × 10 = 5000 × 5000 elements; chip side d = 500 mm × 200/1000 = 100 mm (a 100 mm × 100 mm chip).

Chapter 2.4 · Lectures 4–5

Sampling, quantisation, storage and interpolation

TB 2.4slides pp. 20–28Quiz-1 Q6 type

A camera sees a smooth, continuous scene. A computer can only store a grid of numbers. This section is about that conversion: where we measure (sampling), how finely we round the brightness (quantisation), how much memory the result takes, how to point at one pixel, and how to invent values between pixels when an image is enlarged or rotated (interpolation). Exam questions: storage and transmission time, linear index, bilinear interpolation of new pixels (Quiz-1 Q6), and older papers’ rms quantisation error.

1Digitising = sampling + quantisation

Two separate roundings turn a smooth picture into a digital image: sampling decides where we measure (only at a grid of points), quantisation decides how precisely we store each measured brightness (only L allowed levels).

Sampling = measuring the brightness only at equally spaced points. More points per inch → finer detail (spatial resolution).

Quantisation = rounding each measured value to the nearest of L allowed grey levels 0, 1, …, L − 1. More levels → smoother shading (intensity resolution).

Example. A sensor reads brightness 0.537 on a 0 … 1 scale. With 3 bits there are 8 levels, 0/7, 1/7, …, 7/7. The nearest is 4/7 = 0.571, so the pixel is stored as 4. The small difference (0.034) is the quantisation error.

Blue: the continuous profile, and its exact value (small blue dot) at each sampling position. Orange: that value snapped to the nearest allowed level (dashed) — the stored pixel. Sampling digitises the coordinates; quantisation digitises the amplitude.
Where you use it: theory questions (“define sampling and quantisation”), and every storage and resolution calculation below.

2How many levels, how many bits, how much memory

With k bits per pixel you can count 2k different grey levels. The memory for the whole image is simply (number of pixels) × (bits per pixel).

\(L=2^k\) levels: 0, 1, …, L − 1k = 1 → 2 levels (black/white), k = 3 → 8, k = 8 → 256.
\(b=M\times N\times k\) bitsrows × columns × bits per pixel; ÷ 8 for bytes.

Example. A 1024 × 1024 image with 256 grey levels: k = 8, so b = 1024 × 1024 × 8 = 8,388,608 bits = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MB.

Transmission time = (all bits to send) ÷ (bits per second). If each 8-bit byte travels with a start bit and a stop bit, every pixel costs 10 bits (textbook 2.9).

k (bits)L = 2^k levelsbrightest value

Where you use it: Quiz-type “how many bits / how long to send” questions, and knowing L − 1 for every histogram and negative question.

3Spatial resolution: how fine is the grid?

Spatial resolution is the smallest detail you can see. It is measured as dots (pixels) per inch (dpi) or line pairs per mm (one dark + one light line = 2 pixels).

The same photo stored with fewer and fewer samples (all shown at the same size): detail disappears and edges become blocky.

Typical values (your slide): newspapers 150–200 dpi, books 300 dpi, art books 300–600 dpi.

Example (textbook 2.5). 2048 pixels must fit across 5 cm = 50 mm → 2048/50 = 40.96 pixels per mm = 20.48 line pairs per mm. To fit 2048 pixels in 2 inches → 1024 dpi.

4Intensity resolution and false contouring

Intensity resolution is the smallest change in brightness you can store. With too few levels, a smooth gradual change of brightness turns into visible flat bands with sudden steps — this artefact is called false contouring.

The same photo with 8, 4, 2 and 1 bits per pixel. At 4 bits and below the smooth sky breaks into bands (your slide: false contouring appears with 4 or fewer bits).

Why: with k bits each step between neighbouring levels is 256/2k of the 8-bit range. At 4 bits a step is 16 levels — big enough for the eye to see as an edge. (Textbook 2.12: if the eye notices steps bigger than 8 levels, contours appear for k ≤ 4.)

5Pointing at a pixel: f(x, y), Mf(i, j) and the linear index α

There are three ways to name the same pixel, and your instructor uses all three. Mixing them up is the most common way to lose marks on an otherwise correct answer.

  • f(x, y): x = row (going down), y = column (going right), both counted from 0. f(0, 0) is the top-left pixel.
  • Mf(i, j): the same image as a matrix, but counted from 1 like normal maths matrices. So Mf(i, j) = f(i − 1, j − 1). In Quiz-1, “Mg(2, 2)” meant g at the second row and second column = position (½, ½) of the enlarged grid.
  • α (linear index): number the pixels one after another going down each column, then the next column (like MATLAB). With m rows: α = m·y + x.

Example (picture: m = 3 rows, n = 4 columns). Pixel f(2, 1): α = 3·1 + 2 = 5. Going back from α = 10: y = 10 ÷ 3 without the remainder = 3, x = remainder = 1 → f(1, 3).

Where you use it: Quiz-1 2026 Q6 (“report Mg(2,2)”) and Q3 (“F(1,1) = MF(2,2)”). Always read twice whether an index is from 0 or from 1.

6Interpolation: inventing values between pixels

When an image is enlarged, rotated or registered, the new pixel positions usually fall between the original pixels, where nothing was measured. Interpolation estimates a value there from the nearby known pixels.

Nearest neighbour: copy the value of the closest pixel. Fast, but blocky.

Bilinear: a weighted average of the 4 surrounding pixels; the closer a pixel, the larger its weight. Smooth, a little blurry. Model: g = a·s + b·t + c·s·t + d.

Bicubic: uses the 16 surrounding pixels; sharpest, used in Photoshop.

\(g=(1-s)(1-t)\,A+(1-s)\,t\,B+s\,(1-t)\,C+s\,t\,D\)A = top-left, B = top-right, C = bottom-left, D = bottom-right pixel; s = how far down (0 … 1), t = how far across (0 … 1). Each weight is the area of the rectangle opposite that corner.

Example. A = 10, B = 20, C = 40, D = 50.
Exact centre (s = t = ½): every weight is ¼ → (10 + 20 + 40 + 50)/4 = 30.
On the top edge midway (s = 0, t = ½): only A and B count → (10 + 20)/2 = 15.
At s = 0.25, t = 0.5: 0.375·10 + 0.375·20 + 0.125·40 + 0.125·50 = 22.5.

The nearer you are to a corner, the bigger the rectangle opposite it, so the more that corner counts.

A 64×64 image enlarged 4× three ways.

How zooming works (your slide’s toy example): to enlarge 500×500 to 1000×1000, imagine a 1000×1000 grid, shrink it so it lies exactly over the original image, give every grid point a value by interpolation, then stretch the grid back to full size.

Where you use it: Quiz-1 2026 Q6 (enlarge a 4×3 image to 7×5, report one new pixel). At the exact centre the bilinear answer is just the average of the four corners.
What this lab is. An interpolation calculator. Type a small image and a point (x, y) that is between pixels (fractions allowed); it shows the four neighbouring pixels, the four weights, the bilinear value and the nearest-neighbour value, and the whole 2× enlarged image.
Try this:
  1. Try the exact centre of four pixels (x.5, y.5): all four weights are 0.25 → the plain average.
  2. Try a point on an edge (e.g. 0, 0.5): only two weights are non-zero → the average of two pixels.
  3. Move the point towards one corner: that corner’s weight grows towards 1.

Questions on sampling, storage and interpolation

Practice

Linear index of a pixel

In a 5 × 7 image (m = 5 rows, n = 7 columns), what is the linear index α of pixel f(3, 4)? And which pixel has α = 22?
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here
  1. α: 5×4+3EXE → 23.
  2. Inverse: 22÷5EXE → 4.4: the whole part 4 is y; x = 22 − 5×4 = 2.
Final answer
\(\alpha = 5\cdot4+3 = 23\). For α = 22: \(y = \lfloor22/5\rfloor = 4\), \(x = 22 - 20 = 2\) → f(2, 4).
Full solution
Concept
Column-major stacking: each full column contributes m entries before you reach column y.
  1. \(\alpha = my+x = 5\times4+3 = 23\).
  2. Invert: \(y = \lfloor\alpha/m\rfloor\), \(x = \alpha \bmod m\): \(22 = 5\cdot4+2\) → (x, y) = (2, 4).
Answer
\(\alpha = 5\cdot4+3 = 23\). For α = 22: \(y = \lfloor22/5\rfloor = 4\), \(x = 22 - 20 = 2\) → f(2, 4).
Common mistakes
  • Using n instead of m (m = number of rows multiplies y).
  • Row-major thinking (α = n·x + y) — that is C order, not your slide.

  1. Fast: (10+20+40+50)÷4EXE → 30.

\(M_g(2,2) = g(\tfrac12,\tfrac12) = 30\).
Full solution, step by step
1
Draw the enlarged grid
Insert a new row between every two rows and a new column between every two columns: 4×3 becomes 7×5. Blue = the 12 original pixels (unchanged). The new pixels are of three kinds.
2
Translate the index
Mg(2, 2) is counted from 1: second row, second column of the 7×5 grid. That is a purple pixel — between f(0,0), f(0,1), f(1,0), f(1,1) — at original-grid position (½, ½).
3
Bilinear through the four corners
Fit g = a x + b y + c x y + d through the four corners: (0,0) → 10 gives d = 10; (0,1) → 20 gives b = 10; (1,0) → 40 gives a = 30; (1,1) → 50 gives 30 + 10 + c + 10 = 50, so c = 0.
4
Evaluate at (½, ½)
g = 30·½ + 10·½ + 0 + 10 = 15 + 5 + 10 = 30. (Shortcut: at the exact centre bilinear = average of the four corners = (10 + 20 + 40 + 50)/4 = 30.)
Mg(2, 2) = g(½, ½) = 30.
Faster in the exam
  • Never solve the 4×4 system at a centre point: it is always the plain average of the four corners.
  • For an edge midpoint, average the two pixels it sits between.

Common mistakes

Line pairs per mm and dots per inch for a 2048 × 2048 image

A 2048 × 2048 image must be printed (a) in a 5 cm × 5 cm space: what resolution in line pairs per mm is needed? (b) in 2 × 2 inches: how many dpi?
Final answer
(a) 2048 pixels ÷ 50 mm = 40.96 pixels/mm → 20.48 line pairs/mm. (b) 2048 ÷ 2 = 1024 dpi.
Full solution
1
5 cm = 50 mm. Pixels per mm = 2048 ÷ 50 = 40.96.
2
A line pair is one dark and one light line = 2 pixels → 40.96 ÷ 2 = 20.48 line pairs per mm.
3
Dots per inch = 2048 pixels ÷ 2 inches = 1024.
Answer
(a) 2048 pixels ÷ 50 mm = 40.96 pixels/mm → 20.48 line pairs/mm. (b) 2048 ÷ 2 = 1024 dpi.

Textbook 2.9

How long to send 500 images?

Transmission uses packets of a start bit, a byte (8 bits) of data and a stop bit. (a) How long to send 500 images of 1024 × 1024 pixels with 256 levels over a 3 M-baud line (3×10⁶ bits/s)? (b) Over a 30 G-baud line?
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here
  1. 500×1024x²×10÷3×10ˣ6EXE → 1747.626 s; ÷60EXE → 29.13 min.
  2. (b) Replace 3×10⁶ by 3×10¹⁰ → 0.1748 s.
Final answer
(a) \(500\times1024^2\times10/(3\times10^6) = 1747.6\) s ≈ 29.1 min. (b) \(500\times1024^2\times10/(3\times10^{10}) = 0.175\) s.
Full solution
Concept
256 levels = 8 bits per pixel; each byte travels with a start and a stop bit, so 10 bits on the line per pixel.
  1. Pixels: \(500\times1024\times1024 = 5.243\times10^8\).
  2. Bits on the line: ×10 = \(5.243\times10^9\).
  3. (a) ÷ 3×10⁶ = 1747.6 s ≈ 29.1 min.
  4. (b) ÷ 3×10¹⁰ = 0.1748 s.
Answer
(a) \(500\times1024^2\times10/(3\times10^6) = 1747.6\) s ≈ 29.1 min. (b) \(500\times1024^2\times10/(3\times10^{10}) = 0.175\) s.
Common mistakes
  • Using 8 bits per pixel and forgetting the start/stop bits.

Textbook 2.12

Highest k that still shows false contouring

A flat area lit by \(i(x,y)=255\,e^{-[(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2]}\) (reflectance 1) is quantised with k bits. The eye notices a jump of 8 grey levels between neighbouring pixels. What is the highest k that still causes visible false contouring?
Final answer
k = 4. With k bits the step between levels is 256/2k; it is visible when the step exceeds 8: 256/2k > 8 ⇔ 2k < 32 ⇔ k ≤ 4.
Full solution
Concept
The intensity varies smoothly; quantisation turns it into flat bands with jumps of one quantisation step. Contours are seen when one step is bigger than what the eye can ignore (8 levels).
1
k bits split 0…255 into 2k levels → step ≈ 256/2k.
2
k = 5: step 8 (not more than 8 → not visible). k = 4: step 16 > 8 → visible.
3
Highest visible k = 4. (This matches the slides: false contouring shows at 4 or fewer bits.)
Answer
k = 4. With k bits the step between levels is 256/2k; it is visible when the step exceeds 8: 256/2k > 8 ⇔ 2k < 32 ⇔ k ≤ 4.
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 2:30 (allotment 3:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.

7Quantisation error (older papers): rms error and rms SNR

After quantisation every pixel is a little off. The rms error summarises how far off on average; the rms signal-to-noise ratio compares the size of the signal with the size of that error.

  1. Quantise each value (4 bits on 0 … 255: keep the multiple of 16 just below it, i.e. drop the last 4 bits).
  2. Error e = quantised − original for each pixel.
  3. rms error = √(average of e²).
  4. rms SNR = √( Σ quantised² ÷ Σ e² ).

Mini example: values 37 and 250 → quantised 32 and 240 → errors −5, −10 → e² = 25, 100 → rms error = √(125/2) = 7.91; SNR = √((32² + 240²)/125) = √(58624/125) = 21.66.

State your quantiser in one line (truncation to multiples of 16, or mid-point +8) — the answer depends on it.

Where you use it: Mid-sem 2018-19 Q6 and Mid-sem 2023 Q3 (both older instructor).
Mid-sem 2018-19 Q6 (older instructor)

RMS error and RMS SNR after 4-bit quantisation

An 8-pixel line {255, 118, 129, 182, 18, 178, 82, 53} is uniformly quantised with 4-bit accuracy. Compute the rms error and the rms signal-to-noise ratio of the quantised data.
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here
  1. Statistics app, 1-Variable: type the 8 errors (−15, −6, …, −5) in x.
  2. OK→Statistics Calc then CATALOG→Statistics→Summation→Σx² EXE → 335. (TOOLS→1-Var Results also shows Σx² and n.)
  3. Main screen: √(335÷8)EXE → 6.4711. Re-enter the quantised values to get Σx² = 157440, then √(157440÷335)EXE → 21.68.
Final answer
Quantised (truncate to a multiple of 16): 240, 112, 128, 176, 16, 176, 80, 48. Errors: −15, −6, −1, −6, −2, −2, −2, −5; Σe² = 335. erms = √(335/8) = 6.4711; SNRrms = √(Σf̂²/Σe²) = √(157440/335) = 21.68.
Full solution
Concept
4-bit uniform quantisation of 0…255 keeps 16 levels, 16 apart: keep the top 4 bits (drop the bottom 4) → each value becomes the multiple of 16 just below it. Then compare quantised and original values (the textbook’s “fidelity criteria”).
Formula
\(e_{rms}=\sqrt{\tfrac1N\sum(\hat f-f)^2},\qquad SNR_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sum \hat f^{2}}{\sum(\hat f-f)^2}}\)
1
Quantise: \(\hat f = 16\lfloor f/16\rfloor\): 255→240, 118→112, 129→128, 182→176, 18→16, 178→176, 82→80, 53→48.
2
Errors \(\hat f-f\): −15, −6, −1, −6, −2, −2, −2, −5. Squares sum to 225+36+1+36+4+4+4+25 = 335.
3
\(e_{rms}=\sqrt{335/8}=6.4711\).
4
\(\sum\hat f^2 = 157440\) → \(SNR_{rms}=\sqrt{157440/335}=21.678\) (≈ 26.7 dB if asked in dB: 20 log₁₀ 21.68).
Answer
Quantised (truncate to a multiple of 16): 240, 112, 128, 176, 16, 176, 80, 48. Errors: −15, −6, −1, −6, −2, −2, −2, −5; Σe² = 335. erms = √(335/8) = 6.4711; SNRrms = √(Σf̂²/Σe²) = √(157440/335) = 21.68.
Faster in the exam
  • Errors are just −(f mod 16): 255 mod 16 = 15, 118 mod 16 = 6, … so no subtraction needed.
  • Aim for 12:30 (allotment 15:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Rounding to the nearest multiple of 17 (that is “scale to 16 levels”, a different quantiser). State your rule: “uniform 4-bit quantiser, keep top 4 bits”. If the intended reconstruction is the mid-point of each bin (+8), the answer becomes erms = 5.2797, SNR = 27.90.

Chapter 2.5 · Lecture 5

Neighbours, adjacency, paths and distances

TB 2.5slides pp. 29–30, 51–52past-paper favourite

This topic answers three simple questions about pixels: which pixels are “next to” each other, when you can walk from one pixel to another using only certain grey values, and how far apart two pixels are. The exam asks: the shortest 4-, 8- and m-path between two pixels, how many connected pieces a set of pixels has, and D4, D8, De between two pixels. Everything is done by hand on a small grid — no calculator, no formulas beyond counting.

Coordinates used everywhere below: a pixel is written (row, column), both counted from 0, row 0 at the top. So (3, 0) is the bottom-left pixel of a 4×4 image. This is the same as f(x, y) in your slides: x = row, y = column.

1Neighbours of a pixel: N4, ND, N8

The neighbours of a pixel p are the pixels right around it. There are two kinds: the 4 that share a side with p, and the 4 that only touch p at a corner.

N4(p) — the 4-neighbours: up, down, left, right.
ND(p) — the diagonal neighbours: the 4 corners.
N8(p) — the 8-neighbours: both together (the whole 3×3 block around p, without p).

Example. p = (2, 3).
N4 = (1, 3), (3, 3), (2, 2), (2, 4)
ND = (1, 2), (1, 4), (3, 2), (3, 4)
N8 = all eight of those.

Border pixels have fewer neighbours: a corner pixel has only 2 four-neighbours and 3 eight-neighbours (the others would be outside the image).
Where you use it: adjacency and paths (below); N8 + p is exactly the 3×3 window of every spatial filter in Chapter 3; N4 is what the 4-neighbour Laplacian adds up.

2Adjacency: neighbours whose values are both “allowed”

First you are told a set V of grey values that count (for example V = {1}: “the white pixels”, or V = {1, 2}: “pixels with value 1 or 2”). Two pixels are adjacent when both values are in V and they are neighbours.

4-adjacent: both in V and side by side (q in N4(p)).
8-adjacent: both in V and side by side or corner to corner (q in N8(p)).

Example (picture, V = {1}; blue = value in V):

  • (0, 0) and (1, 0): both 1, side by side → 4-adjacent (and 8-adjacent).
  • (1, 1) and (2, 2): both 1, only touch at a corner → 8-adjacent but not 4-adjacent.
  • (1, 1) and (2, 1): neighbours, but (2, 1) = 2 is not in V → not adjacent.
  • (0, 0) and (0, 2): both 1, but not neighbours → not adjacent.
Where you use it: every path and component question starts by shading the pixels whose value is in V.

3m-adjacency (mixed): 8-adjacency without the shortcuts that cause double paths

With 8-adjacency a pixel can often be reached two ways at once — directly along a diagonal, and also round the corner through a shared neighbour. m-adjacency keeps only one of them: a diagonal step is allowed only if neither of the two “corner” pixels is in V.

The corner pixels of a diagonal step from a to b are the two pixels that are side-neighbours of both a and b — the other two corners of the little 2×2 square.

Example (V = {1}):

  • Diagonal (1, 1) → (0, 2): its corner pixels are (0, 1) = 1 and (1, 2) = 0. One of them is in V, so you can already go round through (0, 1) → the diagonal is not m-adjacent.
  • Diagonal (1, 1) → (2, 2): corners (1, 2) = 0 and (2, 1) = 0, neither in V. The diagonal is the only way through → it is m-adjacent.
  1. Every 4-adjacent pair is also m-adjacent.
  2. For a diagonal pair, look at the 2 corner pixels.
  3. If at least one corner is in V → no (go round). If both corners are outside V → yes.
Where you use it: “shortest m-path” questions (Mid-sem 2019 Q1, Quiz-1 2021 Q4). Remember it as “diagonal only if there is no corner to go round”.

4Paths and their length

A path from p to q is a chain of pixels, each one adjacent to the next (using 4-, 8- or m-adjacency, whichever the question says). Its length = the number of steps (= number of pixels − 1).

The picture shows an 8-path from p = (3, 0) to q = (0, 3) through pixels in V = {0, 1}. The small numbers are the order of the steps: it has 5 pixels, so its length is 4.

How to find the shortest path by hand (works for 4, 8 and m):

  1. Shade every pixel whose value is in V. Check p and q are shaded — if not, no path exists.
  2. Write 0 on p. Write 1 on every allowed pixel you can reach in one step, 2 on every new pixel one step from a “1”, and so on (like ripples).
  3. The number that lands on q is the length of the shortest path. Walk back from q through decreasing numbers to write the path.
  4. If the ripples stop before reaching q, there is no path — say which pixels block it.
Where you use it: every “shortest 4-/8-/m-path” question. 4-paths are never shorter than 8-paths; m-paths are in between.

5Connected components, regions and boundaries

Pixels of V that you can walk between form one connected component (one “blob”). Counting components = counting separate blobs. The answer depends on the adjacency: diagonal touching joins blobs under 8-adjacency but not under 4-adjacency.

Example (V = {1}). With 4-adjacency there are 5 components (each colour is one). With 8-adjacency the single pixel (2, 2) touches (1, 3) at a corner, so those two blobs merge → 4 components.

Region = a connected set of pixels. Two regions are adjacent if together they form one connected set (some pixel of one is adjacent to some pixel of the other — say which adjacency).

Boundary of a region = its pixels that have at least one neighbour outside the region (red in the last picture; the one inside pixel (2, 2) is not on the boundary).

Where you use it: Quiz-1 2018-19 (components in S1 and S2, are S1 and S2 adjacent?). Method: shade V, then colour each blob with the chosen adjacency.

6Three ways to measure the distance between two pixels

Distances only use the coordinates of the two pixels — the grey values do not matter. Take the row difference Δx and the column difference Δy (ignore their signs).

\(D_e=\sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2}\)Euclidean: the straight-line (ruler) distance.
\(D_4=|\Delta x|+|\Delta y|\)City-block: walk only along rows and columns, like a taxi on a street grid. Pixels at D4 = 1 are exactly N4(p).
\(D_8=\max(|\Delta x|,|\Delta y|)\)Chessboard: moves like a chess king (diagonal steps allowed). Pixels at D8 = 1 are exactly N8(p).

Example. p = (1, 1), q = (4, 5): Δx = 3, Δy = 4.
De = √(9 + 16) = 5, D4 = 3 + 4 = 7, D8 = max(3, 4) = 4.

Always D8 ≤ De ≤ D4. Pixels at the same D4 form a diamond; at the same D8 a square.

Different from paths: D4 and D8 ignore pixel values. The textbook’s Dm is the length of the shortest m-path, so it does depend on the values.
Where you use it: Quiz-1 2021 Q1 (Euclidean and city-block), Quiz-1 2018-19 (D4, D8). Calculator only for De.

Try this:

Questions on pixel relationships

Mid-sem 2019-20 Q1 = Textbook 2.18

Shortest 4-, 8- and m-paths, V = {0,1} and V = {1,2}

Exactly as printed in your paper
Same question, typed out
Image segment (rows top to bottom): \(\begin{bmatrix}3&1&2&1\,(q)\\2&2&0&2\\1&2&1&1\\(p)\,1&0&1&2\end{bmatrix}\). (a) V = {0, 1}: shortest 4-, 8- and m-path between p and q; explain if one doesn’t exist. (b) Repeat with V = {1, 2}.
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here

No calculator needed — a path search. Use it only for distances.

  1. De(p, q) = √(3²+3²)EXE = 4.2426; D₄ = 6; D₈ = 3.
Hint
Shade the pixels in V first. For the m-path, at every diagonal step look at the two “corner” pixels.
Final answer
(a) V = {0,1}: no 4-path; 8-path length 4; m-path length 5. (b) V = {1,2}: 4-path length 6; 8-path length 4; m-path length 6.
Full solution, step by step
1
Shade the pixels allowed by V = {0, 1}
Blue = value 0 or 1. p = (3, 0) and q = (0, 3) are both blue, so paths may exist.
2
4-path (V = {0, 1}): none
Ripple out from p using only up/down/left/right steps: you reach the light-blue pixels and then get stuck. q’s only side-neighbours are (0, 2) = 2 and (1, 3) = 2, both outside V — nothing can step into q from the side. So no 4-path exists.
3
8-path (V = {0, 1}): length 4
Diagonal steps are allowed, so the last step (1, 2) → (0, 3) can cut the corner. Shortest: (3,0) → (3,1) → (2,2) → (1,2) → (0,3), 4 steps.
4
m-path (V = {0, 1}): check every diagonal of the 8-path
Diagonal (3,1) → (2,2): its corner pixels are (3,2) = 1 and (2,1) = 2. (3,2) is in V, so you must go round it → refused. Diagonal (1,2) → (0,3): corners (0,2) = 2 and (1,3) = 2, neither in V → allowed.
5
m-path (V = {0, 1}): length 5
Go round through (3, 2): (3,0) → (3,1) → (3,2) → (2,2) → (1,2) → (0,3), 5 steps — one more than the 8-path.
6
Now V = {1, 2}: shade again, then the 4-path
Different pixels are blue now. Ripple with side steps: up the left column, then along the top: (3,0) → (2,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (0,1) → (0,2) → (0,3), 6 steps.
7
8-path (V = {1, 2}): length 4
Two diagonals shorten it: (3,0) → (2,0) → (1,1) → (0,2) → (0,3), 4 steps.
8
m-path (V = {1, 2}): length 6
Diagonal (2,0) → (1,1): corners (1,0) = 2 and (2,1) = 2 are in V → refused. Diagonal (1,1) → (0,2): corner (0,1) = 1 is in V → refused. With every shortcut refused, the m-path is the same as the 4-path: 6 steps.
(a) V = {0, 1}: no 4-path (q’s side-neighbours are both 2); 8-path length 4; m-path length 5. (b) V = {1, 2}: 4-path length 6; 8-path length 4; m-path length 6.

  • Taking a diagonal in the m-path when a shared 4-neighbour is in V.

Quiz-1 2018-19 Q2 = Textbook 2.14 style

Components, adjacency of S1 and S2, D4 and D8

Exactly as printed in your paper
Same question, typed out
For V = {1}, how many 4-connected and 8-connected components are in S1 and in S2? Are S1 and S2 adjacent (4/8)? Find D4 and D8 between the two boxed pixels. (S1 = the left 4×4 box, S2 = the right 4×4 box; see the printed figure.)
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here

No calculator needed.

  1. D₄ = 3 + 6 = 9, D₈ = max(3, 6) = 6 — count rows and columns on the figure.
Final answer
S1: 1 component (4-) and 1 (8-). S2: 3 4-connected components, 1 8-connected component. S1 and S2 are 8-adjacent, not 4-adjacent (they also are m-adjacent). D₄ = 3 + 6 = 9, D₈ = max(3, 6) = 6.
Full solution, step by step
1
Read the figure
S1 = columns 1–4, S2 = columns 5–8 (rows 0–3). Only pixels with value 1 count (V = {1}). Pixels outside the two boxes (columns 0 and 9) are ignored.
2
Components in S1
Its 1s are (1,3), (2,3) going down, then (3,2), (3,3), (3,4) along the bottom: one connected L-shape with side steps → 1 component with 4-adjacency, and also 1 with 8-adjacency.
3
Components in S2
Three blobs that touch each other only at corners: {(0,7), (0,8)}, {(1,6), (2,6), (2,5)}, {(3,7), (3,8)}. With 4-adjacency corners do not join → 3 components. With 8-adjacency (0,7)–(1,6) and (2,6)–(3,7) join them → 1 component.
4
Are S1 and S2 adjacent?
Look across the border between column 4 and column 5: S1’s (3,4) and S2’s (2,5) touch only at a corner. Their corner pixels (2,4) and (3,5) are both 0. So they are 8-adjacent (and m-adjacent, because no corner pixel is in V) but not 4-adjacent.
5
Distances between the boxed pixels
Boxed pixels (3, 2) and (0, 8): Δx = 3 rows, Δy = 6 columns. D4 = 3 + 6 = 9 (walk 3 up and 6 across); D8 = max(3, 6) = 6 (3 diagonal steps, then 3 across). Values do not matter for distances.
S1: 1 component (4-) and 1 (8-). S2: 3 components (4-) and 1 (8-). S1 and S2 are 8-adjacent (and m-adjacent), not 4-adjacent. D4 = 9, D8 = 6.
Common mistakes
  • Counting a pixel outside the box (the extra row/column) as part of S1 or S2.
  • Forgetting that D₄/D₈ ignore the pixel values.
Textbook 2.19 (homework)

When is the D4 distance equal to the shortest 4-path?

For two pixels p and q: (a) state the condition under which the D4 distance between p and q equals the length of the shortest 4-path between them; (b) is that path unique?
Final answer
(a) When there is a 4-path from p to q whose pixels all have values in V and which only ever moves towards q (a “staircase”: every step reduces |Δx| or |Δy|). Then its length is |Δx| + |Δy| = D4. (b) Not in general: if p and q differ in both x and y there are usually several staircases of the same length; it is unique only when p and q are in the same row or column (one straight path), or when V allows just one staircase.
Full solution, step by step
1
Why D₄ is a lower limit
Every side step changes either the row or the column by 1. To get from p to q you need |Δx| row-steps and |Δy| column-steps, so every 4-path has at least D4 = |Δx| + |Δy| steps.
2
When the shortest 4-path equals D₄
Exactly when some path made only of allowed (V) pixels never moves away from q — a “staircase”. If every staircase is blocked by a pixel outside V, the path must detour and becomes longer than D4.
3
Is it unique?
Usually no: the 3 “up” steps and 4 “right” steps can come in many orders (here 35 different staircases). It is unique only if p and q are in the same row or column, or if V leaves just one staircase open.
(a) When a 4-path of pixels in V exists that only moves towards q (a staircase); its length is then D4. (b) Not unique in general; unique only in special cases (same row/column, or V allows a single staircase).
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 2:30 (allotment 3:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting that D4 ignores pixel values while paths do not.

(b) Not unique in general (the diagonal steps can be placed in different orders); unique when p, q are on the same row, column or diagonal and only that line is in V.

Answer
(a) D8 = max(|Δx|, |Δy|) equals the shortest 8-path length when there is an 8-path of pixels in V that moves diagonally max-wise: each step reduces the larger of |Δx|, |Δy| (diagonal steps while both differ, then straight). (b) Not unique in general (the diagonal steps can be placed in different orders); unique when p, q are on the same row, column or diagonal and only that line is in V.

Chapter 2.6 · Lecture 6

The maths toolbox: arithmetic, sets, geometry, transforms, statistics

TB 2.6slides pp. 31–52affine questions

These are the operations every later chapter uses. You do not need to memorise proofs — you need to know what each operation does to an image, and be able to do the small calculations the exam asks: decide whether an operation is linear, combine images with set or logic operations, move points with a matrix (rotate, scale, shift, shear), find that matrix from three point pairs, and compute a mean and a variance.

1Image arithmetic is pixel by pixel

When you add, subtract, multiply or divide two images, you do it to matching pixels — top-left with top-left, and so on. This is not the matrix product you learned in maths.

Example. Multiply two 2×2 images pixel by pixel (the slides call this the Hadamard product, written A ⊙ B): 1×5 = 5, 2×6 = 12, 3×7 = 21, 4×8 = 32.

The matrix product A·B would give something completely different (rows times columns: 1×5 + 2×7 = 19 …). In image processing “A × B” of two images means the pixel-by-pixel version unless the question says “matrix”.

Where you use it: image averaging, subtraction, shading correction, masks (next block), and the “sum of the Hadamard product” that every filter output is.

2What the four arithmetic operations are used for

Each arithmetic operation has one classic job. The pictures show them on a real photograph.

Add, then divide by K: remove noise

Each shot = true picture + random noise. Averaging keeps the picture and cancels the noise: the noise spread (standard deviation) shrinks by √K. Noise σ = 64, K = 16 shots → 64/√16 = 16; K = 64 → 8.

Subtract: find what changed

Everything that stayed the same becomes 0 (black); only the change remains. Used for change detection and digital subtraction angiography (blood vessels after dye − before dye).

Divide: remove uneven lighting

A badly lit image = true image × shading pattern. If you know (or can measure) the shading, dividing by it gives the evenly lit image back.

Multiply by 0/1: keep only a region

A mask is 1 inside the region of interest and 0 outside; multiplying keeps the region and blacks out the rest.

Results outside 0 … 255? Shift and stretch them back: subtract the smallest value, then multiply by K / (largest value). Example: values −20, 0, 30, 80 → subtract −20 → 0, 20, 50, 100 → × 255/100 → 0, 51, 127.5, 255.

Where you use it: theory questions (“how would you detect a missing part?”, “why does averaging reduce noise?”), textbook 2.25, 2.26, 2.29.

3Linear or not? The one-test method

An operation is linear if it treats a mixture of images the same way as the images themselves: doing it to (2 × image) gives 2 × the output, and doing it to (image1 + image2) gives output1 + output2. If you can find one small example where this fails, the operation is nonlinear.

How to test (always works):

  1. Pick two tiny images f₁, f₂ and two numbers a, b (use a = 1, b = −1 or a = 2).
  2. Left side: mix first, then apply the operation: H(a f₁ + b f₂).
  3. Right side: apply first, then mix: a H(f₁) + b H(f₂).
  4. Equal for every choice → linear. Different once → nonlinear.

Example 1 — sum of the pixels (linear): f₁ = [1 2], f₂ = [3 4]. Sum of (f₁ + f₂) = 4 + 6 = 10; sum f₁ + sum f₂ = 3 + 7 = 10 ✓. Always equal → linear.

Example 2 — maximum (nonlinear, the textbook’s example): f₁ = [0 2; 2 3], f₂ = [6 5; 4 7], a = 1, b = −1.
Mix first: f₁ − f₂ = [−6 −3; −2 −4] → max = −2.
Apply first: max f₁ − max f₂ = 3 − 7 = −4. Different → nonlinear.

Example 3 — squaring each pixel (your slide): (2f)² = 4f², but 2·(f²) = 2f² → nonlinear.

Linear (one test never fails)Nonlinear (one example breaks it)
sum or average over a neighbourhoodmax, min, median
correlation, convolution (every filter with fixed weights)thresholding, |value|, squaring
the DFT, F ↦ A F A (your slide)multiplying or dividing two input images
adding / subtracting imageshistogram equalisation (depends on the image itself)
Where you use it: “Is this operator linear? Justify.” — write the test with tiny numbers; one counter-example is a full answer for “nonlinear”.
Textbook 2.23 (homework)

Sum and difference are linear; product and quotient are not

Show that (a) image summation and (b) image subtraction are linear operations, and (c) image multiplication and (d) image division are not.
Final answer
Treat the operation as an operator on the pair of images, H(f, g). (a) H = f + g: H[a(f₁,g₁) + b(f₂,g₂)] = (af₁+bf₂) + (ag₁+bg₂) = a(f₁+g₁) + b(f₂+g₂) ✓ linear. (b) Same with minus ✓. (c) H = f·g: (af₁+bf₂)(ag₁+bg₂) = a²f₁g₁ + ab(f₁g₂+f₂g₁) + b²f₂g₂ ≠ a f₁g₁ + b f₂g₂ → nonlinear. Numbers: f₁ = g₁ = 1, f₂ = g₂ = 0, a = 2: H(2·input) = 4 but 2·H(input) = 2. (d) f/g: 2f/2g = f/g ≠ 2(f/g) → nonlinear.
Full solution
Concept
Linear = “scale the input, the output scales the same way; add two inputs, the outputs add”. One numerical counter-example is enough to prove nonlinear.
1
Write the definition: \(H[af_1+bf_2]=aH[f_1]+bH[f_2]\).
2
Sum/difference: the terms rearrange into exactly the right side.
3
Product: doubling both images multiplies the product by 4, not 2 → fails homogeneity.
4
Quotient: doubling both images leaves it unchanged, not doubled → fails.
Answer
Treat the operation as an operator on the pair of images, H(f, g). (a) H = f + g: H[a(f₁,g₁) + b(f₂,g₂)] = (af₁+bf₂) + (ag₁+bg₂) = a(f₁+g₁) + b(f₂+g₂) ✓ linear. (b) Same with minus ✓. (c) H = f·g: (af₁+bf₂)(ag₁+bg₂) = a²f₁g₁ + ab(f₁g₂+f₂g₁) + b²f₂g₂ ≠ a f₁g₁ + b f₂g₂ → nonlinear. Numbers: f₁ = g₁ = 1, f₂ = g₂ = 0, a = 2: H(2·input) = 4 but 2·H(input) = 2. (d) f/g: 2f/2g = f/g ≠ 2(f/g) → nonlinear.
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 4:15 (allotment 5:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Saying “multiplying by a fixed mask is nonlinear”: f ↦ f·m (m fixed) is actually linear in f. The nonlinearity is in multiplying two input images.
Textbook 2.24

The median is nonlinear

Show that an operator that returns the median of a set of pixels is nonlinear.
Final answer
Counter-example: A = {0, 1, 4}, B = {4, 1, 0} (pixel by pixel). median(A + B) = median{4, 2, 4} = 4, but median(A) + median(B) = 1 + 1 = 2. They differ → nonlinear.
Full solution
Answer
Counter-example: A = {0, 1, 4}, B = {4, 1, 0} (pixel by pixel). median(A + B) = median{4, 2, 4} = 4, but median(A) + median(B) = 1 + 1 = 2. They differ → nonlinear.
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 1:45 (allotment 2:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.
Common mistakes
  • Picking examples where it happens to work (e.g. sets already sorted the same way) — that proves nothing.

4Set and logic operations on images

Your slides treat an image as a set of points (x, y, z) — position and grey value. Then “complement”, “union” and “intersection” become simple pixel rules. For black-and-white (binary) images they are the familiar AND, OR, XOR, NOT.

Grey images (k bits, L = 2k levels):

  • Complement Ac: every pixel z becomes L − 1 − z — the negative.
  • Union A ∪ B: at each pixel keep the larger value (max).
  • Intersection A ∩ B: keep the smaller value (min).

Example (3-bit, L − 1 = 7): A = [1 5; 7 2], B = [4 3; 6 6].

De Morgan check: (A ∪ B)c = 7 − [4 5; 7 6] = [3 2; 0 1] = Ac ∩ Bc ✓.

Binary images (white = 1): A AND B is white only where both are white; A OR B where either is; A XOR B where exactly one is; NOT A swaps black and white; A \ B (difference) = A AND (NOT B).

Where you use it: short computations on 2×2 or 3×3 grey images, and the negative (Chapter 3).
Practice (slide definitions)

Set operations on 3-bit grey images

3-bit images \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\7&2\end{bmatrix}\), \(B=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\6&6\end{bmatrix}\). Find \(A^c\), \(A\cup B\), \(A\cap B\), and check De Morgan \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\).
Final answer
\(A^c=\begin{bmatrix}6&2\\0&5\end{bmatrix}\) (7 − value), \(A\cup B=\begin{bmatrix}4&5\\7&6\end{bmatrix}\) (pixelwise max), \(A\cap B=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\6&2\end{bmatrix}\) (min). \((A\cup B)^c=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=A^c\cap B^c\) ✓.
Full solution
Concept
For grey images (your slides): complement = L − 1 − z (the negative), union = max, intersection = min, pixel by pixel.
Answer
\(A^c=\begin{bmatrix}6&2\\0&5\end{bmatrix}\) (7 − value), \(A\cup B=\begin{bmatrix}4&5\\7&6\end{bmatrix}\) (pixelwise max), \(A\cap B=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\6&2\end{bmatrix}\) (min). \((A\cup B)^c=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=A^c\cap B^c\) ✓.
Faster in the exam
  • Aim for 1:45 (allotment 2:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.

5Three kinds of “spatial” operations

Every operation in the spatial domain is one of three kinds, depending on how many input pixels decide one output pixel.

1 · Single pixel

The output at a pixel depends only on that one input value: s = T(z). Example: the negative s = 255 − z turns 200 into 55. All of Chapter 3’s intensity transformations are this kind.

2 · Neighbourhood

The output depends on a small window around the pixel. Example: the 3×3 average of the window on the right is (1 + 2 + … + 9)/9 = 45/9 = 5. All filters are this kind.

3 · Geometric

Pixels move to new positions (rotate, scale, shift, shear) and their values are filled in by interpolation. Next block.

6Moving pixels with a matrix: the affine transformation

A geometric transformation sends every pixel position (x, y) to a new position (x′, y′). The five basic moves — scale, rotate, shift, shear, reflect — each have a 3×3 matrix. To move a point you multiply the matrix by the point written as (x, y, 1).

Below, the grey letter F is the original and the orange F is the result (x = row, pointing down; y = column, pointing right; the dot is the origin):

Scale by cx, cy

\(x'=c_x x,\ y'=c_y y\). Here both 1.5: bigger, same shape. ½ would shrink it.

Rotate by θ

\(x'=x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta\), \(y'=x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta\). θ = 30°, positive = anticlockwise (your slides).

Shift (translate) by tx, ty

\(x'=x+t_x,\ y'=y+t_y\). Here up 1.5 rows, right 1.2 columns.

Vertical shear

\(x'=x+s_v y\), \(y'=y\): points move up/down by an amount that grows with their column → vertical lines stay vertical, horizontal lines tilt.

Horizontal shear

\(x'=x\), \(y'=s_h x+y\): points slide sideways by an amount that grows with their row → horizontal lines stay horizontal, vertical lines tilt.

Reflect

Scaling with one factor −1: here \(y'=-y\), a mirror image about the x-axis.

Why the extra “1”?

Scaling, rotation and shear only multiply x and y by numbers, so a 2×2 matrix is enough for them. A shift adds a constant, and multiplying never adds a constant. The trick: write the point as (x, y, 1). Then the third column of the matrix gets multiplied by that 1 and simply added:

\(x'=a_{11}x+a_{12}y+a_{13}\cdot 1\)so a13 is exactly “add tx”, and a23 is “add ty”. The bottom row 0 0 1 just keeps the 1 as 1, so the result can be fed into the next matrix.

Example. Shift (2, 3) by tx = 5, ty = −1: \(\begin{bmatrix}1&0&5\\0&1&-1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2+5\\3-1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7\\2\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

Several moves in a row = multiply the matrices. The move done first is written last (closest to the point): scale, then rotate, then shift = T · R · S.

Example. Scale ×2, then shift x by +1, applied to (1, 1): scale → (2, 2), shift → (3, 2). In matrices: T·S·(1, 1, 1) = (3, 2, 1). The other order S·T gives (4, 2) — order matters.

Undoing a move = the inverse matrix A−1: scale by 1/c, rotate by −θ (for rotation A−1 = AT), shift by −t.

Finding A from three point pairs (the exam question)

A has 6 unknown numbers (the top two rows). Each point pair (where a point starts, where it lands) gives 2 equations (one for x′, one for y′). So 3 pairs give 6 equations — exactly enough. Two easy ways to solve:

  1. By hand: the first row (a, b, c) only appears in the x′ equations: a·x + b·y + c = x′ for the three points. Subtract the equations from each other to eliminate c. Do the same for the second row with the y′ values.
  2. By calculator: put the three start points as columns of X (with a row of 1s), the three end points as columns of Y; then A = Y X−1 (Matrix app, recipe F in the calculator section).

Forward vs inverse mapping (how a rotated image is actually made). Going forward — “send each input pixel to its new place” — leaves holes and overlaps, because new places are not whole numbers. So programs go backwards: for every output pixel, compute where it came from with A−1, and interpolate the input there (nearest or bilinear, Section 2.4).

Where you use it: End-sem 2022-23 Q2 (A from three pairs, then map a point), textbook 2.36–2.37 (composite moves, inverses), rotation of a point.

Full solution, step by step
1
What is unknown
A has six unknowns: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\). The first row (a, b, c) makes x′, the second row (d, e, f) makes y′. Each of the 3 point pairs gives one equation for each row.
2
Row 1 from the three x′ values
f(1,1) → x′ = 3: a + b + c = 3. f(0,2) → x′ = −1: 2b + c = −1. f(−1,1) → x′ = 1: −a + b + c = 1.
First − third: 2a = 2 → a = 1. First − second: a − b = 4 → b = −3. Then c = 3 − 1 + 3 = 5.
3
Row 2 from the three y′ values
y′ values −4, −1, 0: d + e + f = −4; 2e + f = −1; −d + e + f = 0.
First − third: 2d = −4 → d = −2. First − second: d − e = −3 → e = 1. Then f = −4 + 2 − 1 = −3.
4
Check one pair
(0, 2): x′ = 1·0 − 3·2 + 5 = −1 ✓, y′ = −2·0 + 1·2 − 3 = −1 ✓.
5
(b) Map (6, −8)
x′ = 1·6 − 3·(−8) + 5 = 6 + 24 + 5 = 35; y′ = −2·6 + 1·(−8) − 3 = −12 − 8 − 3 = −23.
(a) \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-3&5\\-2&1&-3\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) f(6, −8) = (35, −23).

Write the rotation for 30°

Forward: where does (4, 2) go?

Final answer
Write each operation as a 3×3 matrix and multiply in reverse order of application (the first operation sits rightmost, nearest the point): (a) \(A=T\,S=\begin{bmatrix}c_x&0&t_x\\0&c_y&t_y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) \(A=R\,T\,S\). (c) \(A=R\,T\,S\,V\) (V = shear). (d) Yes: scale ×2 then move +1 in x takes (1,1) to (3, 2), but move first then scale gives (4, 2).
Full solution
Concept
A point is a column (x, y, 1). Each matrix acts on what is to its right, so the matrix nearest the point acts first.
1
\(T=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&t_x\\0&1&t_y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\ S=\begin{bmatrix}c_x&0&0\\0&c_y&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\Rightarrow TS=\begin{bmatrix}c_x&0&t_x\\0&c_y&t_y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
2
Order check with \(c_x=c_y=2,\ t_x=1\): \(TS(1,1,1)^T=(3,2,1)^T\) but \(ST(1,1,1)^T=(4,2,1)^T\).
3
Matrix products do not commute in general, so the order of operations matters.
Answer
Write each operation as a 3×3 matrix and multiply in reverse order of application (the first operation sits rightmost, nearest the point): (a) \(A=T\,S=\begin{bmatrix}c_x&0&t_x\\0&c_y&t_y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) \(A=R\,T\,S\). (c) \(A=R\,T\,S\,V\) (V = shear). (d) Yes: scale ×2 then move +1 in x takes (1,1) to (3, 2), but move first then scale gives (4, 2).

Inverse geometric transformations

Find the inverse of (a) scaling, (b) translation, (c) vertical and horizontal shear, (d) rotation, (e) a composite translation-then-rotation.
Final answer
(a) scale by \(1/c_x,\ 1/c_y\). (b) translate by \(-t_x,\ -t_y\). (c) shear by \(-s_v\) (resp. \(-s_h\)). (d) rotate by \(-\theta\): \(R^{-1}=R^T\). (e) \((RT)^{-1}=T^{-1}R^{-1}\): first rotate back by −θ, then translate back by −t.
Full solution
Concept
“Undo” each step, last step undone first (like taking off shoes then socks).
1
\(S^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(1/c_x,1/c_y,1)\), \(T^{-1}\) has \(-t_x,-t_y\) in the last column.
2
Rotation: \(\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}\).
3
Inverse of a product reverses the order.
Answer
(a) scale by \(1/c_x,\ 1/c_y\). (b) translate by \(-t_x,\ -t_y\). (c) shear by \(-s_v\) (resp. \(-s_h\)). (d) rotate by \(-\theta\): \(R^{-1}=R^T\). (e) \((RT)^{-1}=T^{-1}R^{-1}\): first rotate back by −θ, then translate back by −t.

7Image registration: lining up two images of the same scene

Two images of the same thing (e.g. MRI and PET of one patient, or satellite photos taken months apart) are slightly shifted, rotated or stretched relative to each other. Registration warps the input image so it lies exactly on top of the reference image.

  1. Pick tie points (control points): the same feature seen in both images, e.g. a corner of a building. You know where it is in the input, (v, w), and in the reference, (x, y).
  2. Assume the bilinear model: \(x=c_1v+c_2w+c_3vw+c_4\), \(y=c_5v+c_6w+c_7vw+c_8\) — eight unknown numbers.
  3. Each tie point gives two equations (one for x, one for y) → 4 tie points give the 8 equations needed.
  4. Use the fitted model to move every input pixel (with interpolation).

Example (the practice card below): tie points (0,0)→(1,2), (0,10)→(2,13), (10,0)→(11,1), (10,10)→(13,12) give c₁…c₄ = 1, 0.1, 0.01, 1 and c₅…c₈ = −0.1, 1.1, 0, 2. So the input point (5, 5) belongs at (6.75, 7) in the reference.

If the result is not good enough: split the images into smaller pieces and register each piece with its own four tie points, or use a higher-order (polynomial) model.

Where you use it: theory (why 4 tie points? what is the model?) and the c₁…c₈ computation (Equation app, Simul Equation with 4 unknowns, twice).

8Image transforms in matrix form (T = A F A)

An image transform (the DFT is one) rewrites an image as a sum of fixed pattern images, with one coefficient per pattern saying “how much of this pattern is in the image”. When the transform is separable and symmetric, all coefficients come out of two matrix products.

\(T=A\,F\,A\) (forward), \(F=B\,T\,B\) (inverse, \(B=A^{-1}\))F = the n×n image, A = the transform matrix (row u holds the 1-D pattern number u). Multiplying on the left transforms every column, on the right every row.

Example (Haar, 2×2): \(A=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(F=\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(T=AFA^T=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}\). The top-left 4 is the average-type term: (4 − 1 + 2 + 3)/2.

Basis images. The same idea one pattern at a time: each coefficient = sum of (pattern × image) pixel by pixel. For 2×2 images the four patterns are “all +”, “left − right”, “top − bottom”, “checkerboard”. The image is rebuilt as Σ coefficient × pattern; keeping only the largest coefficients gives a good approximation — that is how transform compression works.

The DFT is this with complex patterns (cosines and sines); its kernel is separable and symmetric, so FDFT = Dm F Dn (Chapter 4, Quiz-1 Q3).

Where you use it: Compre 2025 Q4 (both parts), Quiz-1 2026 Q3 (DFT by matrices).

9Mean and variance of an image

The mean is the average grey level (overall brightness). The variance (and its square root, the standard deviation σ) measures how spread out the grey levels are (contrast).

\(m=\dfrac{\text{sum of all pixels}}{\text{number of pixels}}\), \(\sigma^2=\text{average of }(z-m)^2\)With a histogram: \(m=\sum_k r_k\,p(r_k)\), \(\sigma^2=\sum_k (r_k-m)^2p(r_k)\), where p(rk) = (number of pixels with level rk) ÷ (all pixels).

Example. Image [1 2; 3 6]: mean = 12/4 = 3; differences from 3: −2, −1, 0, 3 → squares 4, 1, 0, 9 → average = 14/4 = 3.5 = σ²; σ = 1.87.

Why it matters: a dark image has a small mean; a washed-out (low-contrast) image has a small σ. Histogram questions ask for these (Mid-sem 2023 Q1, 2024 Q1).

Calculator: Statistics app, 1-Variable, Freq column = the counts → x̄ and σx (use σx, not sx).

Textbook 2.26 (homework)

Why averaging K noisy images works

With \(g_i(x,y)=f(x,y)+\eta_i(x,y)\) (noise with zero mean, variance \(\sigma_\eta^2\), uncorrelated between images) and \(\bar g=\frac1K\sum_{i=1}^K g_i\), prove (a) \(E\{\bar g\}=f\) and (b) \(\sigma^2_{\bar g}=\sigma_\eta^2/K\).
Final answer
(a) \(E\{\bar g\}=\frac1K\sum E\{f+\eta_i\}=\frac1K\,(Kf+0)=f\). (b) \(\sigma^2_{\bar g}=\frac1{K^2}\sum\sigma^2_{\eta_i}=\frac{K\sigma_\eta^2}{K^2}=\sigma_\eta^2/K\). So the noise standard deviation falls as \(1/\sqrt K\).
Full solution
Concept
Averaging keeps what is the same in every picture (f) and cancels what is random (noise). Two facts used: variance of c·X is c²·var(X); variances of uncorrelated variables add.
1
The mean of a sum is the sum of means; each noise has mean 0.
2
Pull out 1/K: it becomes 1/K² in the variance.
3
K equal variances add to K σ², times 1/K² gives σ²/K.
Answer
(a) \(E\{\bar g\}=\frac1K\sum E\{f+\eta_i\}=\frac1K\,(Kf+0)=f\). (b) \(\sigma^2_{\bar g}=\frac1{K^2}\sum\sigma^2_{\eta_i}=\frac{K\sigma_\eta^2}{K^2}=\sigma_\eta^2/K\). So the noise standard deviation falls as \(1/\sqrt K\).
Faster in the exam
  • Numbers: σ = 64, K = 100 → σ of the average = 64/√100 = 6.4.
  • Aim for 4:15 (allotment 5:00). If you are stuck at double your share, write the formula with symbols and move on.

Running (recursive) average of images

If a(k) is the average of k images, show how to get the average of k + 1 images from a(k) and the new image fk+1.
Final answer
\(a(k+1)=\dfrac{k\,a(k)+f_{k+1}}{k+1}=a(k)+\dfrac{f_{k+1}-a(k)}{k+1}\).

10Norms and distance functions (appendix of the slides)

A norm measures the size of a vector; the distance between two points is the norm of their difference. The three norms in your slides are exactly the three pixel distances of Section 2.5.

Example x = (3, −4):

  • 1-norm ‖x‖₁ = |3| + |−4| = 7 (→ D4)
  • 2-norm ‖x‖₂ = √(9 + 16) = 5 (→ De)
  • ∞-norm ‖x‖∞ = max(3, 4) = 4 (→ D8)

Always ‖x‖∞ ≤ ‖x‖₂ ≤ ‖x‖₁ (4 ≤ 5 ≤ 7). The points with norm 1 form a diamond (1-norm), a circle (2-norm), a square (∞-norm).

Frobenius norm of a matrix: square every entry, add, take the square root (the 2-norm of the matrix written as one long vector).

A distance function (metric) must (1) never be negative and be 0 only for the same point, (2) be symmetric: d(p, q) = d(q, p), (3) obey the triangle rule: going via r is never shorter, d(p, q) ≤ d(p, r) + d(r, q). De, D4, D8 all satisfy these.

Inner product ⟨x, y⟩ = x₁y₁ + … + xnyn; ‖x‖₂ = √⟨x, x⟩.

Chapter 3.1–3.2 · Lectures 7–8

Intensity transformations: changing each pixel’s brightness

TB 3.1–3.2slides pp. 3–14Quiz-1 Q2 · bit planes

An intensity transformation changes every pixel by the same rule, looking only at that pixel’s own value: new value s = T(old value r). It is the simplest kind of image processing — no neighbours involved. You will be asked for: the negative, a log or gamma value, a piecewise-linear (contrast-stretching) transformation, thresholding, slicing, and especially bit planes (including Gray code and “keep the top k planes”).

1The idea: a rule s = T(r), drawn as a curve

Because T only looks at one value, it is just a lookup table: for every possible input level r (0 … L − 1) it says the output level s. Drawing that table gives a curve — and the curve tells you at a glance what happens to the image.

How to read a transformation curve:

  1. Input r is on the horizontal axis, output s on the vertical axis. The dashed diagonal is “do nothing” (s = r).
  2. Curve above the diagonal → those pixels get brighter; below → darker.
  3. Where the curve is steeper than the diagonal, nearby grey levels are pushed apart → more contrast in that range. Where it is flatter, levels are squeezed together → less contrast.

Your slides call the general form \(g(x,y)=T\{f(j,k)\mid(j,k)\in S_{xy}\}\) — the output at (x, y) computed from a neighbourhood Sxy. An intensity transformation is the special case where Sxy is just the single pixel (1×1).

Monotonic (slide term): a curve that never goes down (r₁ < r₂ ⇒ T(r₁) ≤ T(r₂)) keeps the brightness order of pixels. Strictly monotonic (always going up) also never merges two levels into one, so it can be undone.

2The basic transformations, one by one

Each one has a typical use. Every example below is the same photograph run through the curve next to it.

Negative: s = L − 1 − r

Black ↔ white. 8-bit: r = 200 → s = 255 − 200 = 55. Used to see white or grey detail inside dark regions (mammograms).

Log: s = c · log(1 + r)

Spreads out the dark levels, squeezes the bright ones. Choose c so 255 → 255: c = 255 / log(256) = 105.89 (with log₁₀). Then r = 10 → 105.89·log₁₀11 = 110.3; r = 100 → 212.2. Used to display Fourier spectra (values from 0 to millions).

Power law (gamma): s = c · rγ

Work with r scaled to 0 … 1, then multiply back by 255. γ < 1 brightens the dark parts; γ > 1 darkens. Example r = 64: (64/255)0.4 × 255 = 147; (64/255)2.5 × 255 = 8. Used for gamma correction of displays and for MRI contrast (your slide).

Linear (affine): s = a·r + b

Scale and shift: a > 1 increases contrast, b brightens. Example a = 1.5, b = −20: r = 100 → 130. Values that leave 0 … 255 are clipped.

Where you use it: one-line calculations (Quiz style) and “what does this curve do?” questions.
What this lab is. Shows an intensity transformation s = T(r) as a curve and applies it to a grey ramp (black → white), so you can see what it does to every grey level at once.
Try this:
  1. Choose “negative”: the curve goes down; the bottom strip is the top strip reversed.
  2. Choose “gamma” with γ = 0.4 then γ = 2.5: below 1 brightens the dark part, above 1 darkens it.
  3. Choose “contrast stretch” and move r1, r2 closer together: the steep middle part = more contrast there.

Read the curve: input on the horizontal axis, output on the vertical. Steeper than the dashed 45° line = that range of greys gets more contrast; flatter = less.

3Piecewise-linear transformations: contrast stretching, thresholding, slicing

Instead of a formula, the curve is made of straight pieces joining a few given points. You can then shape exactly which range of greys gets more contrast.

Contrast stretching through (r₁, s₁) and (r₂, s₂): the middle piece is steep (more contrast between r₁ and r₂), the outer pieces flat.

  • Full stretch (your slide): (r₁, s₁) = (rmin, 0), (r₂, s₂) = (rmax, L − 1): the darkest pixel becomes 0, the brightest L − 1. Formula: \(s=(L-1)\dfrac{r-r_{min}}{r_{max}-r_{min}}\).
  • Thresholding: r₁ = r₂ (a vertical jump), s₁ = 0, s₂ = L − 1 → a black-and-white image. Your slide thresholds at the mean intensity.
  • Identity: r₁ = s₁, r₂ = s₂ (nothing changes).

Evaluating any broken line (exam method): find which piece r is in; slope = Δs/Δr of that piece; s = sstart + slope × (r − rstart). Example with the Mid-sem 2019 points (0,0), (30,20), (180,210), (255,255): r = 100 is in the middle piece, slope 190/150 = 1.267 → s = 20 + 1.267 × 70 = 108.67.

Low contrast comes from poor lighting, a sensor with little dynamic range, or a wrong lens aperture (your slide).

Intensity-level slicing: highlight one range of greys

  • Binary slicing: one value (e.g. white) for the range of interest [A, B], another (black) for everything else.
  • With background preserved: brighten (or darken) only [A, B]; every other level stays as it was.

Your slide’s example: highlighting the blood vessels in an aortic angiogram.

Where you use it: Mid-sem 2019 Q6 (the broken line), textbook 3.1 (full stretch), Compre 2025 Q6 (thresholds), slicing theory.

4Bit planes: splitting an image by binary digit

Every pixel is stored as a binary number. An 8-bit pixel has 8 binary digits; take the same digit from every pixel and you get a black-and-white image called a bit plane. Plane 7 (the most significant bit, MSB) is worth 128, plane 0 (the least significant bit, LSB) is worth 1.

Example. 214 = 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 1101 0110. So this pixel is 1 in planes 7, 6, 4, 2, 1 and 0 in planes 5, 3 and 0 (read the digits left to right as planes 7 … 0).

Bit k of r without converting the whole number: divide r by 2k, drop the decimals; if the result is odd, bit k is 1. Example bit 4 of 214: 214/16 = 13.4 → 13 is odd → 1.

Rebuild the image: r = Σ 2k × (plane k). Keeping only the top t planes = keep the top t binary digits, set the rest to 0 = 28−t × ⌊r / 28−t⌋. Example top 3 planes of 214: 32 × ⌊214/32⌋ = 32 × 6 = 192 (1100 0000).

Why bother? The top planes carry the visible structure, the bottom planes look like noise. Keeping only the top 4 planes already looks almost like the original — 50 % less storage (your slide’s compression question).

Gray code (asked in Mid-sem Oct 2024)

In Gray code, neighbouring values differ in exactly one bit, so a tiny change in brightness flips only one bit plane. Rule: g = b XOR (b shifted right by one place). XOR gives 1 where the two bits differ.

Example 6 = 110: shifted = 011; 110 XOR 011 = 101. The Gray MSB always equals the normal MSB.

Full solution, step by step
1
Quantise to 8 bits = round every value
Each value is rounded to the nearest whole number 0 … 255. Row 1 (the second row, counted from 0): 223.78 → 224, 45.3 → 45, 166.9 → 167, 95.87 → 96, 71.4 → 71.
2
Keep the top 3 bit planes
Top 3 planes = keep the first three binary digits (worth 128, 64, 32) and set the rest to 0. Same as 32 × (value ÷ 32 with decimals dropped).
224 = 11100000 → 11100000 = 224
45 = 00101101 → 00100000 = 32
167 = 10100111 → 10100000 = 160
96 = 01100000 → 01100000 = 96
71 = 01000111 → 01000000 = 64
3
Add up row 1
224 + 32 + 160 + 96 + 64 = 576.
Row 1 of g = [224, 32, 160, 96, 64]; Σ g(1, y) = 576.

The intensity transformations that produce the bit planes

(a) Give the transformation functions that produce each bit plane of an 8-bit image. (b) How many for 16-bit images? (c), (d) Does it work when the number of levels is not a power of 2?
Final answer
(a) Plane k (k = 0 for LSB … 7 for MSB): \(T_k(r)=\left\lfloor r/2^k\right\rfloor \bmod 2\) — a staircase that is 0 for 2k values, 1 for the next 2k, and so on (LSB: 0 for even r, 1 for odd r; MSB: 0 for r < 128, 1 for r ≥ 128). (b) 16 functions. (c) It works for any integer levels: write r in binary with ⌈log₂L⌉ bits. (d) Only the number of planes changes; the top planes are then never fully used.
Full solution
Concept
“Bit k of r” means: divide by 2k, drop the decimals, and look at whether the result is odd.
Answer
(a) Plane k (k = 0 for LSB … 7 for MSB): \(T_k(r)=\left\lfloor r/2^k\right\rfloor \bmod 2\) — a staircase that is 0 for 2k values, 1 for the next 2k, and so on (LSB: 0 for even r, 1 for odd r; MSB: 0 for r < 128, 1 for r ≥ 128). (b) 16 functions. (c) It works for any integer levels: write r in binary with ⌈log₂L⌉ bits. (d) Only the number of planes changes; the top planes are then never fully used.
